items.title: The False Net
items.question: Four paper shapes: a cross of five squares plus one attached to an arm; a staircase of two offset rows of three; a row of four with one square above the second and one below the third; a solid 2×3 rectangle. Which CANNOT fold into a closed cube?
items.correctExplanation: The 2×3 rectangle — it lacks the spine-of-four every cube net needs, so faces collide instead of closing. The other three are classic valid nets (cross, 3-3 staircase, 1-4-1).
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the solid 2×3 rectangle. Cube nets need four squares in a wraparound band; the rectangle's 2+2+2 stacking leaves two faces missing and two doubled. Cross, staircase, and mixed-row all contain valid folding spines.
items.lessonContent:
Nets need a wraparound spine of four.
Count the band before trusting the shape.
Rectangles stack; cubes wrap — different topologies.
Invalid nets collide faces instead of closing.
Share this: cut one net and fold it tonight.

items.title: The Southern Pip
items.question: A standard die (opposite faces sum to 7) shows 5 on top and 3 facing north. Which number faces south?
items.correctExplanation: 4 — north-south are opposites, so south is 7 minus 3. Top-bottom (5-2) never enters the calculation.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 4. Opposite pairs sum to 7: north 3 forces south 4, whatever sits on top. Top-bottom information is pure distractor here.
items.lessonContent:
Opposite pairs sum to seven, always.
North-south ignores top-bottom entirely.
Distractor faces test focus, not knowledge.
Pair before placing on every die question.
Share this: orient one die three ways fast.

items.title: The Rolling Census
items.question: A die shows 1 on top, 2 north, 3 east. It rolls east, then north, then east (tipping over each edge in turn). What number ends on top?
items.correctExplanation: 6 — track faces through three tips: east puts 4 up... precisely east (top 4), north (top 5), east (top 6). Rolling permutations compose exactly.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 6. Trace it: roll east (west face 4 rises to top), roll north (south face 5 rises), roll east (west face 6 rises). Each tip swaps four faces; composition does the rest.
items.lessonContent:
Tips permute four faces and fix two.
Track tops through each roll stepwise.
Composition replaces visualization reliably.
East-then-north-then-east has one answer.
Share this: roll one die through three tips.

items.title: The Punched Layers
items.question: A sheet is folded in half, then in half again (four layers), and a hole is punched through all layers near the folded corner. Unfolded, how many holes show?
items.correctExplanation: 4 — one punch through four layers makes four holes, mirrored across both fold lines. Layers multiply punctures exactly.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 4. Each fold doubles the layers (2, then 4), and one punch marks every layer once. Unfolding mirrors the single hole across both creases into four.
items.lessonContent:
Folds multiply layers; punches multiply holes.
Doubling twice quarters the paper into four.
Mirror across every crease to count.
Layers-times-punches is the whole formula.
Share this: punch one twice-folded sheet.

items.title: The Right-Angle Count
items.question: Between 12:00 and 12:00 (twelve hours), how many times do a clock's hands form an exact right angle?
items.correctExplanation: 22 — right angles occur every ~65.45 minutes, twice per hour except the 2–4 stretch merges... precisely 22 in twelve hours (the 11th hour contributes none separately).
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 22. Twice hourly suggests 24, but the 2–3 and 3–4 right angles... the relative hand laps 11 times per 12 hours, yielding 22 perpendiculars. Overlapping cycles steal two from naive counting.
items.lessonContent:
Naive doubling overcounts cyclic events.
Relative laps (11 per 12h) set the true count.
Perpendiculars come in pairs per lap.
Count cycles, not hours, for hand puzzles.

items.title: The Surface Shortcut
items.question: An ant walks on the surface of a unit cube from one corner to the farthest opposite corner. What is the shortest surface distance?
items.correctExplanation: √5 — unfold two adjacent faces into a 1×2 rectangle; the straight diagonal spans √(1+4). Surfaces flatten before measuring.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is √5 units. Through-space (√3) is forbidden; unfold two faces flat and the corner-to-corner straight line crosses a 1-by-2 rectangle. Flatten, then measure — never before.
items.lessonContent:
Unfold surfaces before measuring shortcuts.
Rectangles replace cubes for path problems.
Straight lines on unfoldings are shortest paths.
Through-space answers betray surface rules.
Share this: unfold one box and draw the diagonal.

items.title: The Dawn Polygon
items.question: At sunrise, with light aimed along a cube's body diagonal, what shape is the cube's shadow on flat ground?
items.correctExplanation: A regular hexagon — all six faces project equally around the diagonal axis. Symmetry of viewpoint dictates symmetry of shadow.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a hexagon. Face-on light gives squares, but diagonal light balances all six faces into six equal projected edges. Viewpoint symmetry transfers to shadow shape.
items.lessonContent:
Viewpoint symmetry dictates shadow symmetry.
Diagonal views balance all six faces equally.
Six edges project where four stood.
Rotate the light, reshape the shadow.
Share this: shine one diagonal shadow tonight.

items.title: The Orbiting Coin
items.question: A coin rolls without slipping once around an identical stationary coin. How many full rotations does the rolling coin complete?
items.correctExplanation: 2 — the center travels a circle of twice the radius (4πr path over 2πr circumference). Revolution adds to rotation: one for rolling, one for orbiting.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 2 rotations. Equal circumferences suggest one, but the center's orbit contributes a second full turn. Rolling-plus-revolving sums where pure rolling stands alone.
items.lessonContent:
Orbits contribute rotations beyond rolling.
Center-path length divided by circumference counts.
Equal coins double, never single.
Revolution plus rotation always sums.
Share this: roll one coin around another.

items.title: The Inner Orbit
items.question: A coin rolls without slipping inside a ring of twice its diameter. How many rotations before returning to start?
items.correctExplanation: 1 — inside, the orbit subtracts: center path πd over circumference πd... precisely (R−r)/r = 1. Interior rolling halves the exterior count.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 1 rotation. Inside the ring, revolution opposes rolling instead of adding: the hypocycloid of ratio 2:1 is a straight diameter, and the coin spins once. Outside doubles, inside singles.
items.lessonContent:
Interior orbits subtract where exterior add.
Hypocycloids encode the subtraction exactly.
Ratio 2:1 draws diameters, not loops.
Inside-versus-outside flips the count.
Share this: roll one coin inside a ring.

items.title: The Lifted Rope
items.question: A rope hugging Earth's equator is lengthened by exactly 1 meter, then lifted uniformly all around. How high does it hover?
items.correctExplanation: About 16 centimeters — gap equals extra length over 2π regardless of planet size (1/2π m). Earth's radius cancels completely out.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is about 16 centimeters. Circumference grows 2π per unit radius, so 1 meter buys 1/2π ≈ 0.16 m — on any sphere from marble to Jupiter. Bigness cancels; only the extra meter matters.
items.lessonContent:
Radius cancels out of gap problems entirely.
Extra-over-2π is the universal hover formula.
Planet size never enters the answer.
Linearization defeats astronomical intuition.
Share this: lift one rope around one ball.

items.title: The Moon Fold
items.question: Standard paper (0.1 mm thick) folded repeatedly doubles each time. How many folds reach past the Moon (~384,400 km)?
items.correctExplanation: 42 — 0.1mm × 2⁴² ≈ 440,000 km clears the Moon; 41 folds fall short at ~220,000 km. Exponentials humble linear intuition.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 42. Doubling 42 times multiplies thickness by four trillion; 41 folds reach only halfway to the Moon. Each fold is a doubling, and doublings compound violently.
items.lessonContent:
Doublings compound beyond all intuition.
Forty-two doublings bridge Earth to Moon.
Linear guesses fail exponential questions.
Count doublings, never thickness, first.
Share this: fold one paper seven times max.

items.title: The Caged Sphere
items.question: What is the edge length of the largest cube that fits inside a unit sphere (diameter 2)?
choices: The square root of two units
items.correctExplanation: Two over root three — the cube's space diagonal must equal the diameter: edge times root three equals 2. Corners touch sphere exactly at maximum fit.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is two over root three units. The limiting constraint is the body diagonal spanning the full diameter; edges follow by division. Inscribed means corners-kissing, and kissing sets the equation.
items.lessonContent:
Diagonals, not edges, meet container walls.
Body-diagonal-equals-diameter constrains cubes.
Corners-kissing sets every fit equation.
Divide diagonals to recover edges.
Share this: cage one cube in one sphere.

items.title: The Painted Edges
items.question: A cube is painted red, then sliced into 27 equal small cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two painted faces?
items.correctExplanation: 12 — the edge-centers excluding corners: 12 edges × 1 middle cube each. Two-face cubes live strictly mid-edge.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 12. Corners take three faces (8), face-centers take one (6), leaving edge-middles with exactly two: one per edge, twelve edges. Position classifies paint counts completely.
items.lessonContent:
Position classifies paint counts completely.
Corners three, edges two, faces one, core zero.
Count by location class, never by guessing.
Twelve edges means twelve two-facers.
Share this: dice one painted cube mentally.

items.title: The Single Twist
items.question: A paper Möbius band is cut along its center line all the way around. What results?
items.correctExplanation: One loop twice as long (with two full twists) — the center line never meets an edge to separate. Half-twist topology refuses division.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is one longer loop. The cut rides the band's single surface without ever crossing an edge, so nothing separates — the band survives doubled in length, doubly twisted. One-sidedness preserves unity.
items.lessonContent:
Center cuts ride surfaces without separating.
One-sided bands refuse to become two.
Length doubles where division was expected.
Topology overrides scissor intuition.
Share this: cut one Möbius band tonight.

items.title: The Utility Tangle
items.question: Three houses must each connect to water, gas, and electricity with lines that never cross. On flat ground, is this possible?
items.correctExplanation: No — K3,3 is provably nonplanar (Kuratowski): no crossing-free drawing exists on a plane. Curves don't help; only a handle (torus) would.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is no, the graph is nonplanar. K3,3 defeats every layout trick — straight, curved, clever — on flat ground. Impossibility here is theorem, not lack of trying.
items.lessonContent:
Impossibility can be theorem, not effort shortage.
K3,3 defeats all planar layouts provably.
Curves never rescue nonplanar graphs.
Handles (torus) change the game entirely.
Share this: tangle three houses on paper.

items.title: The Tower Move
items.question: The Tower of Hanoi with 6 disks must move as a stack between pegs, never placing larger on smaller. What is the minimum move count?
items.correctExplanation: 63 — 2⁶−1 by the recursive optimum: move 5 (31), shift the largest (1), rebuild 5 (31). Doubling-plus-one governs every disk added.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 63. The recurrence M(n) = 2M(n−1)+1 with M(1)=1 yields 63 for six disks. Off-by-one answers (64, 32) forget the largest disk's single move or miscount the base.
items.lessonContent:
Recurrence M(n)=2M(n−1)+1 governs towers.
Move n−1, shift largest, rebuild n−1.
Doubling-plus-one punishes every added disk.
Minimums prove by recursion, not experiment.

items.title: The Cornerless Board
items.question: Opposite corners are removed from a chessboard, leaving 62 squares. Can dominoes (each covering two adjacent squares) tile it exactly?
items.correctExplanation: Impossible — removed corners share a color, leaving 32 of one and 30 of the other; each domino needs one of each. Color counts veto the tiling absolutely.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is impossible by color imbalance. Opposite corners match colors, so 62 squares split 32-30 while dominoes demand equality. Invariants beat attempts: no arrangement overcomes arithmetic.
items.lessonContent:
Invariants veto constructions absolutely.
Color counts check tilings before attempts.
Dominoes demand equality square by square.
Removed corners unbalance the whole board.
Share this: color one mutilated board tonight.

items.title: The Block Tower
items.question: Cubes stack: a full 3×3 bottom layer, a centered 2×2 middle layer, and one cube centered on top. How many cubes total?
items.correctExplanation: 14 — 9 + 4 + 1, every cube visible or supporting. Layer sums replace 3D visualization.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 14. Count by layers: 9 below, 4 mid, 1 crown. Centered stacking hides nothing here — all support is visible in the layer below.
items.lessonContent:
Layer sums replace 3D visualization.
Count strata, never guess wholes.
Centered stacks hide nothing structural.
Nine-four-one is the classic pyramid.
Share this: stack one pyramid and count aloud.

items.title: The Spun Word
items.question: The word HOW is rotated 180° in the plane (each letter turns, and their order reverses). What do you read?
items.correctExplanation: MOH — W becomes M, O stays O, H stays H, and reversed order gives M-O-H. Rotation transforms letters and positions together.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is MOH. Rotate each glyph (W→M, O→O, H→H) and reverse their order: W-O-H becomes M-O-H. Letter rotation plus position reversal compose the reading.
items.lessonContent:
Rotations transform glyphs and orders together.
W→M while H,O survive the half-turn.
Reverse positions after turning letters.
Compose both moves before reading.
Share this: spin one word 180 degrees.

items.title: The Inside Glove
items.question: A right-hand glove is turned completely inside out. Which hand does it now fit?
items.correctExplanation: The left hand — inside-out reverses chirality like a mirror. Thumb switches sides with the flip.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the left hand. Eversion mirrors handedness: the thumb that pointed left now points right. Inside-out is a reflection, and reflections swap chirality.
items.lessonContent:
Eversion mirrors handedness exactly.
Inside-out acts as a reflection operator.
Thumbs switch sides with the flip.
Chirality swaps under mirror operations.

items.title: The Polyhedron Census
items.question: A convex polyhedron has 12 vertices and 20 faces. By Euler's formula (V − E + F = 2), how many edges?
items.correctExplanation: 30 — 12 − E + 20 = 2 gives E = 30. Euler counts what eyes cannot.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 30. Plug into V − E + F = 2: 12 − E + 20 = 2, so E = 30. The dodecahedron-icosahedron family lives at these numbers.
items.lessonContent:
Euler's formula counts the uncountable.
Plug vertices and faces; edges emerge.
V−E+F=2 governs all convex solids.
Arithmetic replaces visualization here.
Share this: census one die by Euler.

items.title: The Mirror Planes
items.question: How many planes of mirror symmetry does a perfect cube have?
items.correctExplanation: 9 — three through opposite face-centers plus six diagonal planes through opposite edges. Symmetry exceeds the obvious three.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 9. Beyond the three axis-aligned midplanes hide six diagonal ones, each slicing through opposite edges. Cubes out-symmetricize intuition by exactly six.
items.lessonContent:
Cubes hide six diagonal symmetries.
Axis planes are only the obvious three.
Opposite edges define the secret six.
Count all mirrors, not just straight ones.
Share this: slice one cube diagonally in mind.

items.title: The Inner Diagonal
items.question: What is the length of the space diagonal of a unit cube (corner to farthest corner through the interior)?
choices: The square root of three units
The square root of two units
items.correctAnswer: The square root of three units
items.correctExplanation: The square root of three — face diagonal root two plus unit edge, by Pythagoras twice. Interiors exceed faces exactly so.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the square root of three units. Pythagoras applied twice: face diagonal root two, then root-three through the body. Face diagonals undercount interiors; go one dimension deeper.
items.lessonContent:
Pythagoras applies twice for body diagonals.
Faces undercount interiors systematically.
√2 then √3 climbs dimensions stepwise.
Depth adds its own square every time.
Share this: thread one diagonal through a box.

items.title: The Locked Loop
items.question: Seven gears are meshed in a closed loop, each driving the next. Can they all rotate together?
items.correctExplanation: No — each mesh reverses direction, so seven reversals demand a gear spin both ways at once. Odd loops contradict; even loops turn.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is no, odd loops lock. Meshing flips rotation each step; after seven flips the last gear must match the first yet oppose it. Parity vetoes the motion before friction matters.
items.lessonContent:
Meshing flips direction at every joint.
Odd counts demand impossible self-opposition.
Parity vetoes motions friction never sees.
Even loops turn; odd loops testify.
Share this: loop five coins and watch them jam.

items.title: The Circle Division
items.question: Points on a circle are all joined: 1 point gives 1 region, 2 give 2, 3 give 4, 4 give 8, 5 give 16. Six points give how many?
items.correctExplanation: 31 — the doubling breaks: interior intersections coincide, stealing one region from 32. Pattern 1-2-4-8-16 tempts powers of two; geometry answers 31.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 31. Five points yield 16, but the sixth forces interior triple-concurrency... precisely, intersections stop being generic and one region vanishes. Famous sequences break where intuition naps.
items.lessonContent:
Famous sequences break at the sixth term.
Doubling tempts; geometry corrects.
Interior coincidences steal whole regions.
Test the next term before trusting patterns.
